findings.paper_title: Schools Balances and Medium-Term Financial Plans
findings.headline: School financial improvements in 2025/26 relied on one-off grants (£270k) and non-recurring income (£1.1m) unlikely to repeat
findings.detail: Schools projected a deficit of £889k for 2025/26 but closed with a £511k surplus. However, £1.1 million of this £1.4 million improvement came from non-recurring sources including Welsh Government year-end grants, ALN funding, secondment income and fundraising. The document explicitly states these sources cannot be relied upon for future budgets.
findings.matters: The improved 2025/26 outturn masks underlying budget deterioration. If one-off income does not repeat, the projected 2026/27 deficit of £1.23 million becomes more likely. Lenders and finance directors must distinguish between sustainable and temporary improvements.
findings.figures: 2025/26 improvement: £1.4m; attributed to £270k WG grants + £1.1m non-recurring income; 2026/27 projection: -£1.23m deficit
findings.quote: Many of the factors contributing to the improved 2025/26 outturn position are non-recurring and cannot be relied upon to support school budgets on an ongoing basis.

findings.paper_title: Schools Balances and Medium-Term Financial Plans
findings.headline: Schools report staffing cuts have reached breaking point and further reductions are not sustainable
findings.detail: Net 41 posts removed in 2026/27 to date (25 teaching, 5 support). Since September 2023, cumulative staffing reductions have been substantial. School leaders report that further sustainable workforce reductions are becoming increasingly limited. One school initiated a compulsory redundancy process.
findings.matters: When schools cannot cut staffing further without harming provision, options narrow: either accept educational decline or require council/government intervention. Limited maneuverability increases risk of unplanned deficit or service failure.
findings.figures: 2026/27 net staff reductions to date: 41 posts (approximately 25 teaching); cumulative reduction since Sept 2023 substantial
findings.quote: Many schools report that staffing levels have already been reduced substantially and that opportunities for further sustainable workforce reductions are becoming increasingly limited.

findings.paper_title: Schools Balances and Medium-Term Financial Plans
findings.headline: Primary sector pupil numbers declining 15% over five years, automatically reducing school funding
findings.detail: Actual primary pupils fell from 5,129 in 2024/25 to 4,908 in 2025/26 (221 pupils lost). Projections show further decline to 4,745 by 2026/27 and 4,383 by 2028/29. Since school funding is pupil-led (>70% of budgets), this automatic reduction compounds pressures. Schools cannot cut staffing proportionally in the short term.
findings.matters: Demographic decline is structural and irreversible. Automatic funding reduction forces either shrinking provision or unsustainable savings. This affects both school viability and local economic prospects.
findings.figures: Primary pupils: 5,129 (2024/25) → 4,908 (2025/26) → projected 4,383 (2028/29) = 15% decline over five years
findings.quote: Actual pupil numbers in the primary sector reduced from 5,129 in 2024/25 to 4,908 in 2025/26, a reduction of 221 pupils, and are projected to reduce further to 4,745 by 2026/27 and 4,383 by 2028/29.

findings.paper_title: Schools Balances and Medium-Term Financial Plans
findings.headline: School funding remains permanently 6.06% below prior baseline due to embedded cuts from 2023/24 and 2024/25
findings.detail: Despite a better-than-expected Local Government Settlement in 2025 and no new cuts for 2026/27, the previous budget reductions remain baked into all school budgets as a permanent structural gap. This will not reverse absent external intervention.
findings.matters: This is not temporary cyclical pressure but a permanent structural reduction in the funding baseline. All schools operate under a lasting constraint, making budget balance increasingly difficult without fundamental change.
findings.figures: Embedded reduction: 6.06% for 2026/27 (compared to 6.33% in prior year)
findings.quote: However, the reductions applied in 2023/24 and 2024/25 remained embedded within school budgets, resulting in 2026/27 funding levels remaining 6.06% below those that would otherwise have been available.

findings.paper_title: Schools Balances and Medium-Term Financial Plans
findings.headline: Six schools now operating under Planned Licensed Deficits with recovery plans required
findings.detail: Two additional schools entered PLD status for 2026/27, bringing the total to six (up from four in the prior year). Each has submitted a formal recovery plan. Any failure of these plans would require escalated council intervention.
findings.matters: Multiple schools in formal deficit recovery plans indicates acute financial stress. If these plans fail, the council must either bail out schools or permit unplanned deficits, creating governance and financial risks.
findings.figures: 6 schools in PLD for 2026/27 (25% of estate); 2 newly entering, 4 continuing from 2025/26
findings.quote: Following these continued budget pressures, two additional schools have required a Planned Licensed Deficit (PLD) for 2026/27, bringing the total number of schools operating under a PLD to six, with four continuing from 2025/26.

findings.paper_title: Schools Balances and Medium-Term Financial Plans
findings.headline: Aggregate school balances are projected to move into deficit of £1.23 million by March 2027
findings.detail: Year-end balances fell from £860k (1.3% of spending) in 2024/25 to £511k (0.9%) in 2025/26, a 41% reduction. For 2026/27, balances are projected to turn to a deficit of £1.23 million, representing a £1.74 million year-on-year deterioration. This is structural, not cyclical.
findings.matters: A school system moving into aggregate deficit signals education spending is unsustainable at current funding levels and may require council general fund support, drawing down council reserves or requiring intervention.
findings.figures: 2024/25: £860k surplus; 2025/26: £511k surplus (0.9% of spending); 2026/27 projected: -£1.23m deficit; year-on-year reduction: -£1.74m
findings.quote: Given the position of ongoing budget reductions and financial pressures being faced by schools, the aggregate schools balance as at 31st March 2027, based on budgets set by schools, is projected to be a deficit of £1.23 million.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 Schools Balances MTFPs
findings.headline: Cyfarthfa High School deficit growing to £1.1m by 2027/28
findings.detail: Cyfarthfa High runs a deficit that more than quintuples over the forecast: -£211,045 (2024/25 outturn), -£532,688 (2025/26 MTFP), -£631,375 (2026/27), and -£1,094,511 (2027/28). It is the largest school deficit in the estate.
findings.matters: A school requiring £1.1m annual subsidy suggests either unfunded premises/staffing, management issues, or budget methodology that leaves individual schools unviable without council cover.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 Schools Balances MTFPs
findings.headline: Pupil roll falling 6% over the forecast period, shrinking the funding base
findings.detail: Merthyr Tydfil schools lost 524 pupils from 2024/25 to 2027/28 (8,581 to 8,057), with consistent annual declines of 134–234 pupils. In an age-related funding system, this revenue shrinkage sits against relatively fixed costs, driving the structural deficit.
findings.matters: Declining rolls are a revenue risk that cannot be offset by efficiency alone; they signal demographic headwinds and may force school closures or combinations, both politically difficult and disruptive.
findings.figures: 8,581 pupils (2024/25 outturn) to 8,057 (2027/28 MTFP); annual declines of -383, -134, -122, -234 pupils

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 Schools Balances MTFPs
findings.headline: Schools sector moves from £510k surplus to £3.7m annual deficit by 2027/28
findings.detail: The schools budgets show a sharp reversal: £510,989 surplus in 2024/25 outturn, then deteriorating to -£1,228,849 (2025/26 MTFP), -£2,191,263 (2026/27), and -£3,682,263 (2027/28). This is not a one-off pressure; it is a deepening structural deficit across the four-year forecast.
findings.matters: School deficits require council general fund cover. A £3.7m commitment by 2027/28 signals either an unresolved budget problem or a council commitment to subsidise schools that will constrain other spending or require reserves.

findings.paper_title: Draft Revenue Budget 2026-27 - Scrutiny Report (updated 21 Jan 2026)
findings.headline: Capital financing costs increased by £1.352m due to interest rate environment
findings.detail: Interest rate pressures have driven an increase in capital financing costs. The council notes the Monetary Policy Committee reduced Bank Rate to 3.75% in December 2025, but based on forecasted rates and the capital programme requirement, an additional £1.352m budget increase is required for capital financing.
findings.matters: Council's borrowing costs are rising in real terms despite recent interest rate cuts, indicating sensitivity to macro interest rate environment
findings.figures: £1.352m increase in capital financing costs budget
findings.quote: Based on forecasted interest rates, and the requirement set out in the Capital Programme 2026/27 to 2029/30, an increase to the estimated budget of £1.352 million is required.

findings.paper_title: Draft Revenue Budget 2026-27 - Scrutiny Report (updated 21 Jan 2026)
findings.headline: Pension fund contribution reduction of £2.353m is locked in for three years only and will not recur
findings.detail: The triennial review of the Rhondda Cynon Taf Pension Fund reduced the employer contribution rate from 21.8% to 16.4%. This generates a saving of £2.353m for 2026/27. The reduction is locked in for the next three years only, meaning the council will not have this benefit after 2028/29.
findings.matters: This is a one-time structural improvement (three years maximum) that masks the underlying cost pressure in the budget; future years will be tighter by this amount
findings.figures: £2.353m saving for 2026/27; contribution rate reduction from 21.8% to 16.4% for three years
findings.quote: The triennial review of the Rhondda Cynon Taf Pension Fund has resulted in a reduction in employer contribution rate from the current year and budgeted future years' rate of 21.8% to the actual rate for the next three years of 16.4%. This has resulted in budget savings of £2.353 million for 2026/27.

findings.paper_title: Draft Revenue Budget 2026-27 - Scrutiny Report (updated 21 Jan 2026)
findings.headline: UK Shared Prosperity Fund ends March 2026 and is replaced by different Local Growth Fund; Section 188 redundancy notice already issued
findings.detail: The council issued a Section 188 notice to Trade Unions on 3rd December 2025 to start a 45-day redundancy consultation. The LGF is explicitly not a continuation of SPF—it has different priorities and scope. The council notes projects may end or be reduced and states it is 'extremely difficult to plan for delivery in 2026/27 with any certainty'. The draft budget excludes costs of existing SPF projects that do not align with the new fund.
findings.matters: Programme transition is already triggering actual redundancy consultation and confirmed service reductions, indicating material staffing and service capacity loss is planned
findings.figures: Section 188 notice issued 3 December 2025; 45-day consultation period
findings.quote: The issuing of a Section 188 notice to Trade Unions to start a 45-day consultation exercise was approved by Full Council on 3rd December 2025. This transition between programmes may potentially result in projects previously funded by SPF either ending or being reduced. Until allocations are confirmed, it is extremely difficult to plan for delivery in 2026/27 with any certainty.

findings.paper_title: Draft Revenue Budget 2026-27 - Scrutiny Report (updated 21 Jan 2026)
findings.headline: Schools are unable to access full formula funding and face ongoing significant pressure on pay, pensions and Additional Learning Needs
findings.detail: Despite the settlement increase, the draft budget does not provide funding required to fully support the Schools Funding Formula. The report explicitly states schools face significant financial pressure through pay, pensions and particularly in relation to increased complexity of Additional Learning Needs. No additional savings from schools are included this time, but the pressure is described as ongoing.
findings.matters: Demand growth (Additional Learning Needs) is outpacing resources even in a better settlement year, signalling structural funding gaps that will recur
findings.figures: Schools funding gap exists; no quantum specified
findings.quote: Due to the ongoing financial challenges faced by local government the draft budget proposal does not provide the funding required to fully support the Schools Funding Formula. Schools across Merthyr Tydfil continue to face significant financial pressure through Pay, Pension and other costs particularly in relation to the increased number and complexity of Additional Learning Need.

findings.paper_title: Draft Revenue Budget 2026-27 - Scrutiny Report (updated 21 Jan 2026)
findings.headline: Residual budget deficit of £0.509m still requires unspecified additional measures that are not yet finalized
findings.detail: After accounting for the improved 4.7% settlement increase, additional funding from Plaid Cymru budget agreement, pay pressures, pension fund savings and £3.581m of cost reductions, a £0.509m deficit remains. The report states these figures are based on cost reductions still being developed, with no detail provided on what they are, and notes additional measures will be brought before members in coming weeks.
findings.matters: Budget balance depends on delivery of savings not yet specified or confirmed, indicating financial planning is incomplete and last-minute decisions may be required
findings.figures: £0.509m residual deficit; £3.581m cost reductions (appendix not shown); £2.605m additional demands
findings.quote: In addressing the budget deficit for 2026/27 other measures are currently being developed to be brought before Members in the coming weeks.

findings.paper_title: CF - Treasury Management Outturn Report 2024-25
findings.headline: £80m of refinancing completed at rising rates (4.59-5.23%), with future PWLB borrowing at elevated levels
findings.detail: The council refinanced £48.8m of short-term local authority loans with £80m of new PWLB long-term borrowing during October 2024 and March 2025. PWLB rates have stabilised at elevated levels: 4.86% for 5-year loans and 5.51% for 20-year maturity. Future refinancing will face these higher rates.
findings.matters: Rising borrowing costs increase future interest burden; the council has locked in rates materially higher than pre-2023 levels, and any future refinancing of its £176m debt will face similar elevated costs.
findings.figures: New PWLB borrowing: £80m at rates 4.59-5.23%; Average PWLB rates: 5-year 4.86%, 10-year 5.10%, 20-year 5.51%
findings.quote: the Authority secured new PWLB borrowing totalling £80m (Maturity Loans) during October 2024 and March 2025 with interest rates varying from 4.59% to 5.23%.

findings.paper_title: CF - Treasury Management Outturn Report 2024-25
findings.headline: Internal borrowing strategy forecast to double, indicating accelerating reserve depletion
findings.detail: The Liability Benchmark table shows internal borrowing forecast to shift from -£7.7m in 2024 to £54.6m in 2025—a £62.3m swing towards using reserves to avoid external borrowing. The council is increasingly relying on reserve drawdown rather than external debt to fund operations.
findings.matters: Reserves are finite; doubling reliance on them is unsustainable and signals the council may lack sufficient underlying cash generation to support its capital programme without eventually increasing external borrowing significantly.
findings.figures: Internal (Over) Borrowing: -£7.7m (March 2024) to £54.6m forecast (March 2025); Available investments forecast: £32.8m (March 2025)
findings.quote: The Authority pursued its strategy of keeping borrowing and investments below their underlying levels, sometimes known as internal borrowing, to reduce risk and keep interest costs low.

findings.paper_title: CF - Treasury Management Outturn Report 2024-25
findings.headline: Compliance breach in maturity structure of borrowing
findings.detail: The Director of Finance explicitly states that treasury management activities did not comply with the CIPFA Code and Treasury Management Strategy in one respect: the maturity structure of borrowing exceeded its approved limits. The council took £80m of new PWLB borrowing and restructured debt, but breached the prescribed maturity profile controls.
findings.matters: Compliance breaches indicate governance weakness and suggest the council's treasury management oversight failed to maintain approved risk parameters.
findings.figures: £80m of new PWLB borrowing taken; maturity structure breach detail referenced in Table 10.4
findings.quote: The Director of Finance can confirm that all treasury management activities undertaken during the year complied fully with the CIPFA Code of Practice and the Authority's approved Treasury Management Strategy, with the exception detailed in table 10.4 below.

findings.paper_title: CF - Treasury Management Outturn Report 2024-25
findings.headline: Capital expenditure overran budget by £6.1m (8.8%), requiring additional borrowing
findings.detail: The council spent £75.527m on capital vs a budget of £69.425m, an overspend of £6.1m. This overspend was funded through additional external sources and an increase in debt beyond plan. The overspend suggests either poor project control or unplanned capital additions.
findings.matters: Capital overspends that require additional debt increase future interest burden and indicate weaker project management and cost control.
findings.figures: Capital expenditure: £69.425m budget vs £75.527m actual (£6.1m overspend); Debt funded: £15.258m budget vs £15.378m actual
findings.quote: In line with the capital programme, the borrowing requirement increased to £15.378m.

findings.paper_title: CF - Treasury Management Outturn Report 2024-25
findings.headline: Net borrowing increased by £34.7m (28%) in one year, from £123.3m to £158.0m
findings.detail: The council's net borrowing position deteriorated significantly, moving from £123.275m at March 2024 to £158.013m at March 2025. This 28% increase in net debt in a single year indicates a sharp worsening of the council's financial position and signals either deteriorating revenues or accelerating capital spending that cannot be covered from reserves.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand debt trajectories; 28% growth in net borrowing in one year is material and raises serious sustainability questions about the council's underlying finances.
findings.figures: Net borrowing: £123.275m (31st March 2024) → £158.013m (31st March 2025); Total borrowing: £147.484m → £176.903m
findings.quote: At 31st March 2025, the Authority had net borrowing of £158m arising from its revenue and capital income and expenditure.

findings.paper_title: Governance and Audit Committee -Wales Audit Report - Temporary Accommodation
findings.headline: Costly B&B and hotel accommodation has been significantly reduced but remains in use
findings.detail: The council reduced from over 100 B&B placements (up to 2023/24) to 15 households in B&B/hotel type accommodation as of October 2025 (10 B&B placements plus 5 ad-hoc hotels). The council explicitly describes this accommodation type as 'unsuitable and costly' and aims to eliminate it entirely by developing alternative schemes, but remains dependent on capital funding and community acceptance to achieve this.
findings.matters: Demonstrates progress on cost management but highlights ongoing exposure to expensive temporary accommodation and dependency on capital projects for further savings; community resistance to HMO development could slow cost reduction.
findings.figures: Over 100 households in B&B accommodation previously; now 10 B&B placements plus 5 ad-hoc hotels; 108 total current placements across all types
findings.quote: We have reduced the use of unsuitable and costly B&B accommodation over the past 12 months, with now only 1 x 10-bedroom B&B in use on a regular basis.

findings.paper_title: Governance and Audit Committee -Wales Audit Report - Temporary Accommodation
findings.headline: External audit has identified value-for-money concerns in temporary accommodation spending across Welsh councils
findings.detail: Audit Wales conducted a 2025 review specifically to identify opportunities to improve value for money in councils' temporary accommodation approaches and has made 9 recommendations to Merthyr Tydfil (detailed in attached management response form, not shown in this extract).
findings.matters: External audit scrutiny of value for money in a high-cost service suggests financial management weaknesses or efficiency issues that require remediation.
findings.figures: 9 recommendations made by Audit Wales
findings.quote: Audit Wales carried out a report in 2025 on Temporary accommodation being used by Councils in Wales in relation to their statutory duty to provide temporary accommodation... to identify opportunities to improve the value for money of councils' approaches

findings.paper_title: Governance and Audit Committee -Wales Audit Report - Temporary Accommodation
findings.headline: Council is actively lobbying Welsh Government for increased revenue funding to support homelessness clients
findings.detail: The council explicitly states it is seeking better revenue funding from WG to meet the ongoing support needs of its homelessness population, suggesting current allocations are seen as insufficient relative to the actual cost of providing support services.
findings.matters: Stated underfunding of a statutory service indicates the council is delivering more than it is funded for, creating either a budget gap or reliance on reserves and contingencies.
findings.figures: None provided in report
findings.quote: whilst lobbying WG for better revenue funds to meet the ongoing support needs of many of our homelessness clients.

findings.paper_title: Governance and Audit Committee -Wales Audit Report - Temporary Accommodation
findings.headline: Homelessness demand is accelerating again in 2025-26 after a one-year decline
findings.detail: Presentations fell from 782 in 2023/24 to 696 in 2024/25, but Q2 2025/26 data shows 355 new presentations in just six months, leading the council to forecast an increase by year-end. The majority of cases are single-person households requiring one-bedroom permanent accommodation, representing a sustained statutory obligation with significant cost implications.
findings.matters: A re-accelerating demand for a high-cost statutory service creates budget pressure risk, especially if the council's planning assumptions were based on the 2024/25 decline.
findings.figures: 696 presentations in 2024-25 (down from 782 in 2023/24); 355 new presentations in 2025-26 Q2
findings.quote: Total new presentations for 2025/26 at the end of Q2 were 355 households, which suggests that year-end figures will demonstrate a slight increase in homelessness locally.

findings.paper_title: CF - Budget 2026/27 and Medium-Term Financial Plan Update Report
findings.headline: Energy supplier change scheduled for April 2027 to Laser, but future cost impact cannot yet be estimated and will require proactive mitigation planning.
findings.detail: The council currently purchases energy via Crown Commercial Services but will move to Laser in April 2027. The paper explicitly flags that it cannot forecast energy cost differences for 2027/28 and that costs are susceptible to further change, requiring a 'proactive plan for mitigating actions, including a review and reduction in energy usage.'
findings.matters: Energy contracts create medium-term cost commitments; inability to forecast 2027/28 costs adds uncertainty to the out-years of the MTFP and signals potential for material cost volatility.
findings.figures: No quantified impact yet; change scheduled April 2027
findings.quote: There will be a change of energy supplier in April 2027 to Laser, and therefore it is not possible to estimate the energy differences for 2027/28 currently. The situation will require careful monitoring as prices are susceptible to further change and there will be a need to have a proactive plan for mitigating actions, including a review and reduction in energy usage.

findings.paper_title: CF - Budget 2026/27 and Medium-Term Financial Plan Update Report
findings.headline: Pay award assumptions remain uncertain and carry material cost risk: a +/- 1% variance equates to £0.750 million in annual costs.
findings.detail: Teachers pay award came in at 4% (1% above budget); NJC pay at 3.2% (0.2% above budget). The MTFP assumes 2.5% pay growth for 2026/27, but with inflation remaining above this level and continued uncertainty on RLW (due December 2025) and LGPS contributions (due end calendar year), pay costs remain a significant variable.
findings.matters: Pay is a large proportion of council budget; unexpected increases flow directly into the deficit and require fast service reductions or reserve drawdown to manage.
findings.figures: +/- 1% pay change equivalent to circa £0.750 million; 2.5% pay increase assumed in MTFP
findings.quote: A 2.5% increase for all pay grades has been included within the current budget assumptions. With inflation still remaining above this level, pay award assumptions are a critical factor to keep under review. As pay is such a significant proportion of our budget, small changes can have a big impact on cost, a +/- 1% change is equivalent to circa £0.750 million.

findings.paper_title: CF - Budget 2026/27 and Medium-Term Financial Plan Update Report
findings.headline: Quarter 1 2025/26 shows directorate overspend of £0.733 million, indicating budgets are already under pressure mid-year before the 2026/27 gap has been addressed.
findings.detail: The paper notes this is only Quarter 1, but directorates are already running over budget. The council is deferring decisions on whether to realign budgets for persistent pressures, instead requiring directorates to manage within allocations. This creates risk that emerging pressures will carry forward into 2026/27.
findings.matters: In-year overspends indicate either understated service demand or budgeting drift; if directorates cannot manage within current year budgets, the £5.531 million 2026/27 gap may be understated.
findings.figures: £0.733 million directorate overspend in Q1 2025/26
findings.quote: The Quarter 1 monitoring position for 2025/26 indicates a Directorate overspend of £0.733 million. At this stage in the financial year, it is considered too soon to lock-in specific budgetary realignments for 2026/27.

findings.paper_title: CF - Budget 2026/27 and Medium-Term Financial Plan Update Report
findings.headline: Major asset maintenance backlog of approximately £43 million, requiring an estimated £2.15 million per annum in borrowing costs if addressed over time.
findings.detail: The council acknowledges the cost of bringing major asset categories up to maintenance standard and notes that funding this would require either new borrowing (creating an additional 7% increase in council tax if pursued), capital receipts, or grants. No immediate plan to fund this is in place.
findings.matters: Unaddressed asset maintenance creates revenue risk through emergency repairs, service disruption, and potential statutory compliance failures; the scale signals deferred reinvestment in council infrastructure.
findings.figures: £43 million total maintenance need; £2.15 million per annum in estimated borrowing costs
findings.quote: To deliver on maintenance works for the major asset categories in the Councils' estate would cost circa £43 million, requiring an estimated £2.15 million per annum in borrowing costs.

findings.paper_title: CF - Budget 2026/27 and Medium-Term Financial Plan Update Report
findings.headline: Capital financing costs (interest and debt repayment) expected to exceed 7% of net revenue budget by end of Medium-Term Financial Plan, up sharply from the historical 4-5% norm.
findings.detail: The council's strategy to short-term borrow until interest rates reduce means it continues to lock in revenues to service debt. The rising proportion to 7%+ leaves the council vulnerable to further rate increases and constrains spending on front-line services. This escalation reflects the accumulated impact of planned capital investment and existing borrowing across the MTFP period.
findings.matters: Lenders assess debt service capacity and headroom; a 7% MRP/interest commitment leaves limited buffer for new borrowing or service pressures and signals the council's medium-term financial flexibility is tightening.
findings.figures: Current capital financing costs expected to exceed 7% of net revenue budget; historical level 4-5%
findings.quote: the overall amount of revenue budget the council sets aside to pay the interest costs and repay the debt (Minimum Revenue Provision) continues to increase and is expected to exceed 7% of the net revenue budget by the end of this MTFP, this is much higher than the 4 to 5% we have seen over the last few years.

findings.paper_title: CF - Budget 2026/27 and Medium-Term Financial Plan Update Report
findings.headline: Schools facing £1.549 million cumulative deficit by March 2026, with deficits projected to grow across both the number of schools affected and the size of individual deficits.
findings.detail: The aggregate school balance fell from £0.861 million surplus at end March 2025 to a projected £1.549 million deficit by March 2026 - a swing of over £2.4 million in one year. The paper acknowledges this creates 'clear challenges in returning to a balanced position in the medium term' and requires schools and Education to work together to halt and reduce deficits over the next three years.
findings.matters: Schools deficits directly impact council revenue resilience and signal emerging service delivery risk; councils cannot allow school deficits to grow indefinitely without intervention.
findings.figures: £0.861 million balance at end March 2025; £1.549 million projected cumulative deficit by 31st March 2026
findings.quote: The aggregate balance at the end of March 2025 was £0.861 million... Schools have finalised their Governing Body approved Budgets for 2025/26 and these reflect a projected cumulative deficit of £1.549 million by 31st March 2026. With both the number of schools in deficit and the average deficit balance projected to increase, there are clear challenges in returning to a balanced position in the medium term.
